reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it discusses and mathematically examines another person's speculative $5,000 BONE price claim rather than presenting a guaranteed return or directing viewers to send money or data. The creator describes the scenario as hypothetical and gives no purchase instruction, payment destination, wallet request, or external-action requirement.

citations.quote: I saw another YouTuber actually. Mention that. They believe that Ethereum could actually be half the price, I'm sorry, bone,. It would be half the price of Ethereum.
so this is just hypothetical guys.
So if we just do just a quick. Cross-multiplication, this would get us down to Bone price being at $11.25.
Can it get to $5,000? Anything's possible in crypto, guys.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the prediction alongside the action available on screen. The title advertises a $5,000 BONE price prediction, while the displayed BONE market page includes a Buy control. The speaker then asks viewers to stay tuned and presents a calculation reaching $11.25. No one explicitly says to purchase, but the combination can steer viewers from a striking appreciation claim to an immediately visible purchase option. That promotional effect deserves weight even without a spoken buying instruction.

so make sure you stay tuned to listen in and understand where I'm. Coming from.
this would get us down to Bone price being at $11.25.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the calculation hypothetical does not erase the audience-facing pairing of a $5,000 headline with a market page that displays a Buy control. The defense is right that the speaker attributes the larger figure to someone else; the concern is that he keeps that figure in view while making the investment case sound worth considering. The absence of a spoken wallet request answers a narrower concern than whether the presentation steers viewers toward a token purchase.

citations.quote: so this is just hypothetical guys.
it is a strong possibility due to the fact that, again, Shibarium is stacked on top of Ethereum.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A Buy control on a market-information page is not a purchase instruction from the speaker. He identifies the $5,000 idea as another creator's, labels his own calculation hypothetical, and explicitly declines to put forward that prediction. The quoted $11.25 calculation shows what he is discussing, not a promised return or a required next step for viewers.

opening.argument: Judge, the risk signal is the cumulative impression. A headline foregrounds $5,000; the speaker says BONE reaching that level is a 'strong possibility' and adds that its price possibilities 'could be infinite.' He also invokes Shibarium, token pairings, the Metaverse, and exchange listing as upward factors. Those claims appear alongside a BONE price page with a Buy control. His qualifications matter, but they do not prevent the presentation from amplifying extraordinary appreciation as a reason to consider buying the token.

citations.quote: $5000 BONE SHIBASWAP TOKEN PRICE PREDICTION... THIS IS CRAZY
it is a strong possibility due to the fact that, again, Shibarium is stacked on top of Ethereum.
Plus, you got the Metaverse. You got exchange listing. It's just so many good factors that go into Bone to the point where the possibilities of prices could be infinite.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes 'hypothetical,' but that qualifier applies to the $11.25 calculation; it does not undo the later description of $5,000 as a 'strong possibility.' Nor does attributing the original idea to another creator remove the speaker's own list of reasons for BONE to rise. The issue is the combined sales-like impression, not whether he guarantees a specific return or gives a wallet address.

citations.quote: so this is just hypothetical guys.
but it is a strong possibility due to the fact that, again, Shibarium is stacked on top of Ethereum.
This would drastically increase the price of Bone. Plus, you got the Metaverse. You got exchange listing.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited enthusiasm is speculative, not an offer of returns. The speaker says he does not see $5,000 happening, calls the calculation hypothetical, and frames his conclusion as thoughts and opinion. A standard market page showing BONE's price and a Buy control does not establish that he directs viewers to buy. The promotional reading relies on tone and juxtaposition, while the actual discussion remains conditional.

opening.argument: Judge, the worked example gives this more than the appearance of casual commentary. The speaker says he likes 'mathematical proof,' displays a handwritten calculation ending at $11.25, and argues that Ethereum's rise would pull BONE upward even without Shibarium or a new listing. He then adds those potential catalysts back into the picture. That sequence uses analysis to build confidence in the token's appreciation; the visible BONE market page supplies a purchase route. The educational format can therefore function as promotion even though the speaker never issues a direct order to buy.

This would drastically increase the price of Bone. Plus, you got the Metaverse. You got exchange listing.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls the cross-multiplication an examination of another person's claim. But the speaker also asserts that BONE would follow Ethereum upward and then supplies additional reasons its price could increase. A disclaimer that the example is hypothetical limits certainty; it does not make the favorable argument disappear. A judge should assess the overall persuasive direction of the presentation, not just the absence of an explicit deposit request.

He also says he would not put out the $5,000 prediction himself. Presenting a speculative model and discussing possible catalysts may influence an audience, but the quoted material does not show him asking viewers to purchase BONE or promising that appreciation will occur.
